title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: A West Michigan city pauses new data centers as concerns over power and water grow statewide.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're talking about a small West Michigan city that just enacted its own temporary halt on new data center proposals, following neighbors down the road.
This feels like it's picking up steam, Graham. What's the bigger picture here with all these pauses?

Exactly. The action stems from worries over heavy demands on local electricity and water supplies that could raise costs for residents. Michigan readers 30-60 miles away should watch how this affects regional utility planning and tax bases as more towns consider limits.
Why are communities suddenly moving on this now? Is there a history we're missing?

It's been building. We've seen similar moves in neighboring communities, and the pattern is spreading. Towns are concerned that big facilities could strain the grid and pull water from aquifers, potentially bumping up everyone's electric bills.
How does that actually play out for regular folks? Like, what kind of numbers are we talking about with power and water use?

A single large data center can draw enormous amounts of electricity—think hundreds of megawatts—and millions of gallons of water daily for cooling. That competes with homes, farms, and businesses on the same systems.
And the farmland angle? These projects often sit on or near agricultural land, right?

Yes, and that raises questions about land use changes, traffic from construction, and long-term tax revenue versus short-term gains. Some places are weighing whether the jobs promised offset the infrastructure hits.
Who are the key players pushing back or moving forward?

Local councils and residents are driving the pauses, often after hearing from utilities or seeing proposals. Developers are still active in spots like Mason County, where two centers broke ground this weekend.
What happens next in these paused towns? Do they just study and then decide?

Most are using the time to update zoning rules and permitting standards. Garfield Township, for example, is spending a full year crafting those guidelines. It gives everyone a chance to model the real impacts first.
And for places 30 or 60 miles away, how might this ripple out?

Regional utilities plan across bigger areas, so one town's limits could shift where the next projects land—or push rates if demand concentrates elsewhere. Tax bases might also see shifts if projects move or get scaled back.
Any sense of how many communities are now in this mode?

It's a growing list: Warren with its year-long halt yesterday, Ypsilanti extending its freeze, Kalamazoo adding a moratorium to its code, and others like Saline Township delaying tax break votes. The trend is clear statewide.
Does this slow the overall buildout or just redirect it?
Both, probably. It buys time for better rules while some projects restart bids, like the old electric plant site. The grid strain concerns aren't going away.
Graham, thanks for laying that out. It really shows why these local decisions matter beyond town borders.
Now let's hit the other stories making moves this week.
Yesterday Warren's city council approved that 12-month moratorium after residents raised alarms over power and water draws in Macomb County.
Gives officials time to study zoning before anything advances. Smart move when the stakes are this high.
On Sunday, recall efforts started targeting a Springfield Township supervisor over data center fights. Residents blame fast-tracking that could strain roads, power, and water.
Shows how these projects are now shaping local politics in southeast Michigan. A successful recall would change who controls approvals.
Also Sunday, Ypsilanti kept its data center freeze in place while studying impacts. Residents want more time before any large projects move ahead.
That could affect rates in Ann Arbor and beyond if approvals come later. Ripple effects are real.
Saline Township delayed its vote on a 12-year tax break for the big Oracle campus. Supervisors postponed action on forgiving taxes for the multibillion-dollar project.
Leaves open whether they'll forgo revenue for roads and schools. Residents are questioning the scale versus promised jobs.
Saturday saw a developer restart efforts at the old Emerson Electric campus site. New power demand questions for the community.
And Mason County broke ground on two major centers that weekend. They'll pull significant electricity and add construction jobs, but locals will feel the grid and tax impacts.
Kalamazoo added a moratorium to its zoning code to slow the rush amid AI proposals.
Gives time to study while statewide grid and water worries grow.
Garfield Township is taking a full year to draft rules on zoning and permitting. Limits on power, noise, and water could come before any projects.
And Friday, Mid-Michigan residents got a first look at the numbers via a university town hall on power and water demands. Concrete megawatts and daily use figures for folks within 30 miles.
Good context for communities questioning developers early.
Now, on deck for listeners who want to weigh in.
Tonight Ypsilanti City Council has the second reading and potential adoption of that 60-day emergency moratorium on data center zoning permits.
Tomorrow, City of Ionia holds an informational meeting on the industry and potential local impacts if proposals come up.
Also tomorrow, University of Michigan is hosting a community town hall on the proposed $1.2 billion high-performance computing facility in Ypsilanti Township.

And next week on the 15th, Ypsilanti City Council has a public hearing on zoning ordinance text amendments for data centers, including definitions and performance standards, plus the emergency moratorium proposal.
Plenty of chances to show up and ask questions.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: West Michigan Joins Data Center Pause Wave
